messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Just first iteration with Hierarchical model responses and response times
parts:
Several issues:

- You'll need to explain your data. I don't understand what you're doing with NA data. It looks like you're only ever asserting sampling when the data is not NA, in which case there's no need to include the NA cases in the first place. Including NA data is usually done when you want to use the non-NA data to infer what the NA data might have been. 

- I also suspect you might be able to get a speedup by using a non-centered parameterization on paramP and paramQ and thereby avoiding looping over them to assert the sampling of their rows individually and instead simply asserting to_vector(paramP_raw) ~ normal(0,1), etc.

- why are you using inv_sqrt(0.001) in the specification of the scale for the normal priors on muP & muQ? Why not just put 30? (Stan gurus: if 30ish is indeed desired as the scale of these priors, should we furthermore expect improved efficiency from a non-centered parameterization where, for example, muP_raw is defined as normal(0,1) and muP is defined in the transformed parameters section as muP_raw*30 ?

- You are computing diag_pre_multiply(sigmaP,L_OmegaP) for every iteration of the outter loop over 1:P, and, worse, computing diag_pre_multiply(sigmaQ,L_OmegaQ) on every inner loop over 1:Q. You should just compute both once, storing the result to a variable that is then referenced inside the loops. 

- You also might try to move all computations you can to the transformed parameters block. For example, here's your code in a cleaned-up format (please try to use consistent spacing) with those cholesky-decomposed covariance matrices computed in the transformed parameters block:

  data {
    int P ; // # Individus
    int Q ; // # Items
    real LogTimesNA[P,Q] ; // Log responses times
    real IndNA[P,Q] ; // NA index  (1 if NA, 0 ifelse)
    int ItemsNA[P,Q] ; // Responses
  }
  parameters {
    vector[2] paramP[P] ; // Parameters of persons (theta,tau)
    vector[2] paramQ[Q] ; // Parameters of items (betaR,betaT)
    vector[2] muP ; // mean of multivariate normal for parameters (theta, tau) of persons
    cholesky_factor_corr[2] L_OmegaP ; 
    real<lower=0> sigmaP2 ; 
    vector[2] muQ ; // mean of multivariate normal for parameters (betaR, betaT) of items
    cholesky_factor_corr[2] L_OmegaQ ; 
    vector<lower=0>[2] sigmaQ ;
    vector<lower=0>[Q] sigmaT ; // variance of Log times
  }
  transformed parameters{
    matrix LP ;
    matrix LQ ;
    {
      // I create vector sigmaP to fix sigmaP[1] = 1
      vector[2] sigmaP ;
      sigmaP[1] <- 1 ;
      sigmaP[2] <- sigmaP2 ;
      LP <- diag_pre_multiply(sigmaP,L_OmegaP)
      LQ <- diag_pre_multiply(sigmaQ,L_OmegaQ)
    }
  }
  model {
    // Priors
    muP ~ normal(0,inv_sqrt(0.001)) ;
    sigmaP2 ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    L_OmegaP ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2) ;
    muQ ~ normal(0,inv_sqrt(0.001)) ;
    L_OmegaQ ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2) ;
    sigmaQ ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    sigmaT ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    for(p in 1:P){
      paramP[p] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(muP,LP) ;
      for(q in 1:Q){
        paramQ[q] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(muP,LQ) ;
        if(IndNA[p,q]==0){
          ItemsNA[p,q] ~ bernoulli_logit(paramP[p,1]-paramQ[q,1]) ;
          LogTimesNA[p,q] ~ normal(paramQ[q,2] - paramP[p,2],sigmaT[q]) ;
        }
      }
    }
  }

Including NA data is usually done when you want to use the non-NA data to infer what the NA data might have been.
I also couldn't follow this.

> - I also suspect you might be able to get a speedup by using a non-centered parameterization on paramP and paramQ and thereby avoiding looping over them to assert the sampling of their rows individually and instead simply asserting to_vector(paramP_raw) ~ normal(0,1), etc.

If there's not a lot of data, non-centering is a win.

The "centering" in question is of both the mean and the log scale
around zero.

>
> - why are you using inv_sqrt(0.001) in the specification of the scale for the normal priors on muP & muQ? Why not just put 30? (Stan gurus: if 30ish is indeed desired as the scale of these priors, should we furthermore expect improved efficiency from a non-centered parameterization where, for example, muP_raw is defined as normal(0,1) and muP is defined in the transformed parameters section as muP_raw*30 ?

Yes, because then muP_raw, which is what's actually being sampled, is
on the unit scale, so we don't have to estimate that scale during
warmup. So warmup should go faster and be more accurate.

> - You are computing diag_pre_multiply(sigmaP,L_OmegaP) for every iteration of the outter loop over 1:P, and, worse, computing diag_pre_multiply(sigmaQ,L_OmegaQ) on every inner loop over 1:Q. You should just compute both once, storing the result to a variable that is then referenced inside the loops.

What you really need to do is vectorize these. That way, even the
Cholesky factor is only factored once.
> - You also might try to move all computations you can to the transformed parameters block. For example, here's your code in a cleaned-up format (please try to use consistent spacing)
+1 on consistent spacing (and no tabs!).
> with those cholesky-decomposed covariance matrices computed in the transformed parameters block:

Computing in the transformed parameters block saves the parameters
in the output, so only define there if you want to save. Otherwise,
you can use a local variable in the model block. Either way, it's
better to just vectorize. Then you can just write the expression directly
inside the call to the density.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Just first iteration with Hierarchical model responses and response times
parts:
Hi,

Thanks for you help.

When submitting a computerized test limited in time to the subjects, we can record two types of informations, responses and responses times that suejts put to answer the various questions of the test.

Items: matrix (P × Q)
Time: matrix (P × Q)

Furthermore, it is known that parameters such topics as competence (theta) which can be estimated from the Items and speed (tau) that can be estimated from the responses times.
It is the same for the items where we can estimate the difficulty of each item with items (betaT) and the time required to answer an item (betaR).

We know that the items (0 and 1) follow a parameter Bernoulli  P = 1 / (1 + exp (theta-betaR)).
It is known that the logarithmic transformation of the response times follow a normal distribution (tau-betaT, sigma)

But the parameters of the subjects (theta and tau) follow a multivariate normal (muP,sigmaP)
and item parameters (BetaR and BetaT) a multivariate normal. (muQ,OmegaQ)

muP = (mu_theta, mu_tau)
sigmaP =(sigma_theta, cov_thetatau, cov_thetatau, sigma_tau)

muQ = (mu_betaR, mu_betaT)
OmegaP =(1, covvar_thetatau, covvar_thetatau, sigma_betaT)
paramP = (theta,tau) , paramQ = (betaR, betaT).

In this data, there are missing data NA. As Stan does not support NA, I have identified the IndNA data.
So I made different cal estimates of observed data by ignoring NA missing data.

I hope to bring explicitations

Bests regards.

Several issues:

- You'll need to explain your data. I don't understand what you're doing with NA data. It looks like you're only ever asserting sampling when the data is not NA, in which case there's no need to include the NA cases in the first place. Including NA data is usually done when you want to use the non-NA data to infer what the NA data might have been. 

- I also suspect you might be able to get a speedup by using a non-centered parameterization on paramP and paramQ and thereby avoiding looping over them to assert the sampling of their rows individually and instead simply asserting to_vector(paramP_raw) ~ normal(0,1), etc.

- why are you using inv_sqrt(0.001) in the specification of the scale for the normal priors on muP & muQ? Why not just put 30? (Stan gurus: if 30ish is indeed desired as the scale of these priors, should we furthermore expect improved efficiency from a non-centered parameterization where, for example, muP_raw is defined as normal(0,1) and muP is defined in the transformed parameters section as muP_raw*30 ?

- You are computing diag_pre_multiply(sigmaP,L_OmegaP) for every iteration of the outter loop over 1:P, and, worse, computing diag_pre_multiply(sigmaQ,L_OmegaQ) on every inner loop over 1:Q. You should just compute both once, storing the result to a variable that is then referenced inside the loops. 

- You also might try to move all computations you can to the transformed parameters block. For example, here's your code in a cleaned-up format (please try to use consistent spacing) with those cholesky-decomposed covariance matrices computed in the transformed parameters block:

  data {
    int P ; // # Individus
    int Q ; // # Items
    real LogTimesNA[P,Q] ; // Log responses times
    real IndNA[P,Q] ; // NA index  (1 if NA, 0 ifelse)
    int ItemsNA[P,Q] ; // Responses
  }
  parameters {
    vector[2] paramP[P] ; // Parameters of persons (theta,tau)
    vector[2] paramQ[Q] ; // Parameters of items (betaR,betaT)
    vector[2] muP ; // mean of multivariate normal for parameters (theta, tau) of persons
    cholesky_factor_corr[2] L_OmegaP ; 
    real<lower=0> sigmaP2 ; 
    vector[2] muQ ; // mean of multivariate normal for parameters (betaR, betaT) of items
    cholesky_factor_corr[2] L_OmegaQ ; 
    vector<lower=0>[2] sigmaQ ;
    vector<lower=0>[Q] sigmaT ; // variance of Log times
  }
  transformed parameters{
    matrix LP ;
    matrix LQ ;
    {
      // I create vector sigmaP to fix sigmaP[1] = 1
      vector[2] sigmaP ;
      sigmaP[1] <- 1 ;
      sigmaP[2] <- sigmaP2 ;
      LP <- diag_pre_multiply(sigmaP,L_OmegaP)
      LQ <- diag_pre_multiply(sigmaQ,L_OmegaQ)
    }
  }
  model {
    // Priors
    muP ~ normal(0,inv_sqrt(0.001)) ;
    sigmaP2 ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    L_OmegaP ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2) ;
    muQ ~ normal(0,inv_sqrt(0.001)) ;
    L_OmegaQ ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2) ;
    sigmaQ ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    sigmaT ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    for(p in 1:P){
      paramP[p] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(muP,LP) ;
      for(q in 1:Q){
        paramQ[q] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(muP,LQ) ;
        if(IndNA[p,q]==0){
          ItemsNA[p,q] ~ bernoulli_logit(paramP[p,1]-paramQ[q,1]) ;
          LogTimesNA[p,q] ~ normal(paramQ[q,2] - paramP[p,2],sigmaT[q]) ;
        }
      }
    }
  }

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Just first iteration with Hierarchical model responses and response times
parts: Ah, so the inclusion of the NA indicator is to maintain a PxQ data matrix amidst missing data. Note that the alternative solution (that would get rid of the need for the if() check in the model) to this is to reformat the data to long format and toss the NA entries, after which you'd have a data section akin to:

data {
     int P ; // # Individus
     int Q ; // # Items

int N ; // total # of non-NA data points
     vector[N] LogTimes ; // Log responses times
     vector[N] Responses ; // Responses
     vector[N] P_label ; // P labels associated with each of the N data points
     vector[N] Q_label ; // P labels associated with each of the N data points
   }

You then need to re-code your model to account for the new data structure. A similar (though only including one random effect where you have two) hierarchical model with long data can be seen here: https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/4989099

If I were you, I'd try our earlier suggestions first, and if you're still sampling slowly, try reformatting to long and tossing the NA data. 

(Stan gurus: would you expect the conversion to long-format to avoid the if() check in the model to be worth it? My intuition on what is more efficient is still sketchy...)

It looks like you're only ever asserting sampling when the data is not NA, in which case there's no need to include the NA cases in the first place. With a iter=1000 run (which takes about 7mins on my machine), most parameters have a good ESS of about 500, with muP and muQ being the exceptions, so it looks like you'd need more iterations for those.     sigmaT ~ invgamma(0.001,0.001);

 for(p in 1:P)

       LogTimesNA[p,q] ~ normal(paramQ[q,2] - paramP[p,2],sigmaT[q]);
     }

Ah, so the inclusion of the NA indicator is to maintain a PxQ data matrix amidst missing data. Note that the alternative solution (that would get rid of the need for the if() check in the model) to this is to reformat the data to long format and toss the NA entries, after which you'd have a data section akin to:

  data {
     int P ; // # Individus
     int Q ; // # Items
     int N ; // total # of non-NA data points
     vector[N] LogTimes ; // Log responses times
     vector[N] Responses ; // Responses
     vector[N] P_label ; // P labels associated with each of the N data points
     vector[N] Q_label ; // P labels associated with each of the N data points
   }

You then need to re-code your model to account for the new data structure. A similar (though only including one random effect where you have two) hierarchical model with long data can be seen here: https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/4989099

If I were you, I'd try our earlier suggestions first, and if you're still sampling slowly, try reformatting to long and tossing the NA data. 

(Stan gurus: would you expect the conversion to long-format to avoid the if() check in the model to be worth it? My intuition on what is more efficient is still sketchy...)

Le mardi 7 juin 2016 17:34:45 UTC+2, Mike Lawrence a écrit :
Several issues:

- You'll need to explain your data. I don't understand what you're doing with NA data. It looks like you're only ever asserting sampling when the data is not NA, in which case there's no need to include the NA cases in the first place. Including NA data is usually done when you want to use the non-NA data to infer what the NA data might have been. 

- I also suspect you might be able to get a speedup by using a non-centered parameterization on paramP and paramQ and thereby avoiding looping over them to assert the sampling of their rows individually and instead simply asserting to_vector(paramP_raw) ~ normal(0,1), etc.

- why are you using inv_sqrt(0.001) in the specification of the scale for the normal priors on muP & muQ? Why not just put 30? (Stan gurus: if 30ish is indeed desired as the scale of these priors, should we furthermore expect improved efficiency from a non-centered parameterization where, for example, muP_raw is defined as normal(0,1) and muP is defined in the transformed parameters section as muP_raw*30 ?

- You are computing diag_pre_multiply(sigmaP,L_OmegaP) for every iteration of the outter loop over 1:P, and, worse, computing diag_pre_multiply(sigmaQ,L_OmegaQ) on every inner loop over 1:Q. You should just compute both once, storing the result to a variable that is then referenced inside the loops. 

- You also might try to move all computations you can to the transformed parameters block. For example, here's your code in a cleaned-up format (please try to use consistent spacing) with those cholesky-decomposed covariance matrices computed in the transformed parameters block:

  data {
    int P ; // # Individus
    int Q ; // # Items
    real LogTimesNA[P,Q] ; // Log responses times
    real IndNA[P,Q] ; // NA index  (1 if NA, 0 ifelse)
    int ItemsNA[P,Q] ; // Responses
  }
  parameters {
    vector[2] paramP[P] ; // Parameters of persons (theta,tau)
    vector[2] paramQ[Q] ; // Parameters of items (betaR,betaT)
    vector[2] muP ; // mean of multivariate normal for parameters (theta, tau) of persons
    cholesky_factor_corr[2] L_OmegaP ; 
    real<lower=0> sigmaP2 ; 
    vector[2] muQ ; // mean of multivariate normal for parameters (betaR, betaT) of items
    cholesky_factor_corr[2] L_OmegaQ ; 
    vector<lower=0>[2] sigmaQ ;
    vector<lower=0>[Q] sigmaT ; // variance of Log times
  }
  transformed parameters{
    matrix LP ;
    matrix LQ ;
    {
      // I create vector sigmaP to fix sigmaP[1] = 1
      vector[2] sigmaP ;
      sigmaP[1] <- 1 ;
      sigmaP[2] <- sigmaP2 ;
      LP <- diag_pre_multiply(sigmaP,L_OmegaP)
      LQ <- diag_pre_multiply(sigmaQ,L_OmegaQ)
    }
  }
  model {
    // Priors
    muP ~ normal(0,inv_sqrt(0.001)) ;
    sigmaP2 ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    L_OmegaP ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2) ;
    muQ ~ normal(0,inv_sqrt(0.001)) ;
    L_OmegaQ ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2) ;
    sigmaQ ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    sigmaT ~ cauchy(0,2.5) ;
    for(p in 1:P){
      paramP[p] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(muP,LP) ;
      for(q in 1:Q){
        paramQ[q] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(muP,LQ) ;
        if(IndNA[p,q]==0){
          ItemsNA[p,q] ~ bernoulli_logit(paramP[p,1]-paramQ[q,1]) ;
          LogTimesNA[p,q] ~ normal(paramQ[q,2] - paramP[p,2],sigmaT[q]) ;
        }
      }
    }
  }
